title: Restless-Legs-Syndrome (RLS)—A Primarily Peripheral-Sensory Disorder? Revisiting the Iron Deficit Hypothesis of RLS
content: Restless-Legs-Syndrome (RLS) is a frequent disorder in sleep medicine which is associated with a variety of predisposing conditions and is oftentimes associated with nocturnal periodic leg movements. While a motoric urge and sensory leg discomfort are necessary sensory symptoms in RLS, night-time periodic leg movement can be regarded as the motoric dimension of RLS and may also occur isolated without day-time symptoms. The heterogeneity of related diseases indicates a common underlying pathomechanism by which the relatively stereotypical symptoms in RLS may be induced. Demonstrating the case of a patient with severe RLS and giving a summary of prevalence studies, a theory of peripheral tissue hypoxia as the main pathophysiological mechanism causing symptoms of RLS is outlined. This pathophysiological model is based on the assumption that peripheral tissue hypoxia may be the main factor in RLS and periodic leg movement disorder resulting in increased afferent input which is relayed to cerebral sensory areas and induces spinal motor reflex circuits. Treatment-wise, this implies that pharmacological treatment of RLS with dopaminergic substances, α2δ-ligands and opioids works by attenuating the enhanced afferent input caused by tissue hypoxia. In addition, the reversal of RLS symptoms by oxygen supplementation, as demonstrated in the presented case, questions the hypothesis a central nervous iron deficit and indicates a working mechanism by improved tissue oxygenation.
